question: A new member asks whether green tea is acceptable under the Word of Wisdom, since it's marketed as a healthy 'herbal' drink. What is the Church's clarified position (per the 2019 New Era statement)?
choices: Green tea is fine because the prohibition on 'hot drinks' refers only to black coffee and black tea, not lighter varieties
Green tea is prohibited because it comes from the same tea plant as black tea, and both green and black tea are off-limits
Green tea is a matter of personal conscience; the Word of Wisdom only bans alcohol, tobacco, and coffee by name
Green tea is acceptable as long as it is served cold or iced rather than hot, since the rule targets 'hot drinks'
source: Newsroom, 'Statement on the Word of Wisdom,' New Era, Aug 2019; D&C 89
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that the prohibition tracks the tea plant (Camellia sinensis), so green AND black tea are both prohibited. The temperature distractor exploits the literal 'hot drinks' wording (folk legalism) — but iced tea is still tea; the 'only named substances' distractor is the permissive Sunstone reading; the 'lighter varieties' option is a near-miss that gets the same-plant logic backwards.

question: In Latter-day Saint practice, what is the basic relationship between tithing and the fast offering?
choices: The fast offering is simply the portion of one's tithing set aside specifically to feed the poor in the ward
Tithing is one-tenth of one's increase paid to the Church; the fast offering is a separate, additional donation—ideally at least the cost of the meals skipped while fasting—used to care for the needy
Both are voluntary suggestions; faithful members may fulfill the obligation by donating either ten percent OR a fast offering, whichever they can afford
Tithing fulfills the law of sacrifice, so members who pay a full tithe are not expected to also contribute fast offerings
notes: Tests understanding that tithing (10% of increase) and the fast offering (a distinct donation tied to monthly fasting, traditionally the value of the meals missed, devoted to the poor) are two separate principles, not interchangeable. The first distractor collapses them into one fund (oversimplification); the third treats them as either/or (heterodox/permissive); the fourth invents an exemption that sounds doctrinally tidy but is false.
